blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: The principle of moments and how to apply it, the two conditions a system must satisfy to be in equilibrium, and the triangle of vectors for three coplanar forces in equilibrium.

blocks.heading: The principle of moments
blocks.text: The principle of moments states the condition for a body not to start turning: for a body in equilibrium, the sum of the clockwise moments about a single point is equal to the sum of the anticlockwise moments about that same point. Three things belong in a complete statement: the two sums, the single point both are taken about, and the equilibrium condition. A see-saw with riders of different weights stays level when the heavier rider sits closer to the pivot, so that the clockwise moments match the anticlockwise moments. The principle is a statement about moments, so it is used alongside the condition that the forces balance.

blocks.heading: Applying the principle
blocks.text: A moments problem is worked in a fixed order. Choose the point to take moments about. Resolve any force that acts at an angle, or measure its perpendicular distance directly. Calculate each moment, and sort them into clockwise and anticlockwise about the chosen point. Then set the sum of the clockwise moments equal to the sum of the anticlockwise moments and solve for the unknown. The point can be chosen freely, and a good choice does half the work: taking moments about a point that an unknown force acts through removes that force from the equation, because its moment about that point is zero. A reaction at a support, for example, vanishes from the equation the moment the support itself is chosen as the point.

blocks.heading: Worked example: a wheelbarrow
blocks.text: A gardener in Windhoek lifts a loaded wheelbarrow. The total weight of barrow and load is 245 N, acting at the centre of gravity, which sits 0.50 m behind the wheel's axle. Her hands on the handles are 1.10 m behind the axle, and she lifts straight upwards with force L. In equilibrium, the moments about the axle balance: clockwise moment of the weight = anticlockwise moment of the lift, so 245 N × 0.50 m = L × 1.10 m. The left side is 245 × 0.50 = 122.5 N m, so L = 122.5 ÷ 1.10 = 111.4 N, which is 110 N to two significant figures. The wheel's upward reaction takes the rest of the weight; it never enters the equation because moments were taken about the axle.

blocks.heading: Equilibrium
blocks.text: A system is in equilibrium when two conditions hold at the same time: the resultant force on it is zero, and the resultant torque on it is zero. Zero resultant force removes any linear acceleration; zero resultant torque removes any starting to rotate. Both conditions must be checked separately, because one can hold while the other fails. Equilibrium is a statement about forces and turning effects, not a description of how fast something happens to be moving.

blocks.heading: At rest is not the whole story
blocks.text: It is tempting to say a body at rest is in equilibrium. Rest by itself shows nothing of the kind. A ball at the top of its flight is momentarily at rest while its weight still acts on it, and a beam supported at one end can have balanced vertical forces yet still be turned by its own weight about the support. The error is concluding equilibrium from rest, or from zero resultant force alone. The test is the two zero resultants, checked separately: the forces must balance, and the moments about a point must balance too. A body at rest in equilibrium stays at rest; a body at rest with a resultant torque on it starts to turn.

blocks.heading: What equilibrium means for the motion
blocks.text: A system in equilibrium does not accelerate and does not begin to rotate. It stays at rest, or keeps moving at a steady velocity in a straight line without starting to turn. The link runs both ways. If both resultants are zero, no push or twist is left over to change the motion. If a system's velocity is steady and its rotation is not changing, the forces on it must balance and the moments about a point must balance, so the system is in equilibrium.

blocks.heading: The triangle of vectors
blocks.text: Three coplanar forces in equilibrium can be drawn as a closed triangle. Draw the first force as an arrow. Draw the second starting head to tail from its tip, parallel to the force and scaled to its size. Draw the third the same way from the tip of the second. Because the arrows return to the starting point, the three forces add to zero: the triangle closes, and a closed triangle of vectors has no resultant. No side of the triangle is a resultant force. Each side is one of the three forces, drawn head to tail; for forces in equilibrium there is no resultant to find.

blocks.heading: Solving with the vector triangle
blocks.text: The angles inside the triangle come from the geometry of the situation, not from the forces themselves. A banner hanging from two ropes is a common case: the ropes make stated angles with the vertical or the horizontal, and those angles set the corners of the triangle once the weight is drawn pointing straight down. With the triangle's angles known, the two unknown force sizes follow by trigonometry: usually the sine rule, or simple cosines if the triangle is right-angled. A rough sketch of the triangle, drawn to scale, doubles as a check on the arithmetic: if the third side does not close the triangle, the two computed forces do not balance the weight.

blocks.heading: Worked example: a banner over a shop
blocks.text: A banner weighing 40 N hangs from a bracket outside a shop in Oshakati. A rope holds it, making an angle of 40° with the vertical, and a horizontal strut pushes out from the wall with force S. The three forces in equilibrium are: the weight 40 N straight down, the tension T along the rope, and the strut's push S horizontal. Drawn head to tail they close as a right-angled triangle: the weight is the side adjacent to the 40° angle, the strut's push is the side opposite it, and the rope's tension is the hypotenuse. So T = 40 N ÷ cos 40° = 40 ÷ 0.766 = 52.2 N, which is 52 N to two significant figures, and S = 40 N × tan 40° = 40 × 0.839 = 33.6 N, which is 34 N to two significant figures. The triangle closes, so there is no resultant: the banner hangs still.

blocks.heading: Where this connects
blocks.text: The vector triangle uses the vector addition of forces from topic 3, where forces were combined into a resultant; equilibrium is the special case where the resultant is zero. The principle of moments rests on the moment of a force from sub-topic 4.1. In topic 6 a body in equilibrium under stretching forces is analysed the same way, and in topic 12 the balance of a suspended object is checked practically at the bench.
